headlines.title: ‘I have a lot to live for': Greg Papa opens up about cancer fight, family and job
headlines.description: In his own words. Greg Papa sat down with NBC Bay Area for his first television interview since recent health complications from his cancer diagnosis. NBC Bay Area’s Raj Mathai met with the legendary broadcaster at his home in Marin County for a wide-ranging interview that focused on facing death, family, being laid off by KNBR and more. “I do not want to die,” Papa said. “I’m going to fight as hard as I can, fight to stay alive. I have a lot to live for.” For decades, Papa’s voice has brought to life some of the most colorful sports moments. He’s given the Bay Area memories that span generations from his time covering the A’s and Raiders to the Warriors, Giants and 49ers. These days, his voice is strong and still resonates, but the game has changed. Doctors diagnosed him with leukemia last summer. He got sick while vacationing in France. “There were many nights there that I felt, you know, I may die,” Papa said. “Cancer is unfair. Cancer is sudden. Cancer is cruel.” His lifeline turned out to be his bloodline. His younger sister, Judy, was a perfect match. In March, she donated her stem cells for a bone marrow transplant. A month later, things took a turn for the worse. Complications from the transplant caused pneumonia, and his lungs collapsed. He nearly died and spent 78 days in the ICU. “I was put on a ventilator,” Papa said. “I was intubated. I was in an induced coma for about five days. It went from a life-threatening situation for certain to a life-altering one…I’ve made a lot of progress since I’ve been home. I made a lot progress since late July.” He continues his fight and wants to get back to what he loves in the radio booth. “I’m cleared, by the way, to go back on the radio show that I had that I no longer have,” he said. In early August, Papa was laid off by KNBR. In his first public comments since the layoff, he said, “I was fully preparing to return to work. There was never discussion that that would not be the case. And then one day you get a phone call and I thought it was a return-to-work plan…I was cleared, my hematologist cleared me [for the radio show] and they went the other way and they chose to terminate my contract.” Cumulus Media, which owns KNBR, issued a statement on Aug. 7 acknowledging Papa’s departure, writing, “our respect and gratitude for everything Greg has given to KNBR, its listeners, and its team runs deep. We are continuing to explore ways we can bring his voice back to the station, and we wish Greg strength, healing, and a full recovery.” Papa still has his job as the San Francisco 49ers radio announcer. He said he’d like to come back sometime this season to call games, but he didn’t know if that was possible. The David Benzer Strike Out Fear Foundation has set up a GoFund Me campaign to help with the financial burden of Papa’s long recovery.
headlines.source: Raj Mathai, Christine Ni and Alex Bozovic

headlines.title: 1 dead after car drives off cliff in Santa Cruz, lands in ocean
headlines.description: One person died and another was injured after they drove off a cliff in Santa Cruz and landed in the ocean early Thursday morning, according to officials. The crash happened at about 12:50 a.m. off West Cliff Drive near the Steamer Lane surfing spot, officials said. One person was able to get out of the car on their own and reach safety, according to officials. They suffered minor injuries. Rescue swimmers jumped into the ocean and were able to pull a second person from the submerged car. Despite life-saving measures, that person later died at the hospital, officials said. Officials did not immediately say who was driving the car when the crash occurred. The cause of the crash is under investigation.

headlines.title: 3.8 magnitude earthquake, multiple aftershocks strike near San Leandro
headlines.description: A 3.8 magnitude earthquake struck near San Leandro Thursday morning, according to the United States Geological Survey. The quake hit at 8:30 a.m. and was centered 2.4 miles north of San Leandro, 4.9 miles north-northwest of Ashland and 5.3 miles south-southwest of Moraga, the USGS said. “It was just like a big jolt,” Alicia Battle of Castro Valley said. “We had a few things knocked over – nothing damaged – but it was pretty strong.” The initial quake was followed by 3.0 and 2.8 magnitude aftershocks at about 9:07 a.m., according to the USGS. No damage was immediately reported. “This is not something unexpected for the Bay Area, especially for this region,” said Dr. Angie Lux, a project scientist for Earthquake Early Warning at the Berkeley Seismology Lab. “It doesn’t mean that we are going to have a big earthquake soon, but we do know at the same time that we are overdue for a large earthquake on the Hayward Fault.” Following the initial earthquake, BART temporarily held trains before allowing them to run at reduced speeds while crews completed safety inspections of the tracks. Normal BART service later resumed, but the agency said there were major residual delays systemwide. headlines.title: ‘Neighbors evicting neighbors': Longtime North Beach tenants fight to stay in their homes
headlines.description: Six North Beach households could lose the apartments they’ve called home for decades after new owners bought their building last year and soon began trying to evict them. Faced with soaring San Francisco rental prices, the tenants say they face an uncertain future and could be forced out of the city they love if they lose their rent-controlled apartments. Yok Lin Chui has lived in the building on Powell Street for more than 50 years after immigrating from Hong Kong in 1971. She said she uses neighborhood buses to get around and has easy access to Chinatown. “I’m so old now, where should I go?” she said through a translator, growing visibly upset when asked what she would do if forced to move. “I don’t know how to take a taxi.” Chui’s neighbor, Meagan Cunningham, moved into the building in 1987 as a child and still lives there with her adult son, Max. She’s a voice-over artist and used to work in a neighborhood restaurant. “This is such a big part of my history, this neighborhood,” she said. “Good times, bad times, but I’ve been here for so long.” But decades of shared history could be coming to an end. Seven new owners bought the building in February of last year through a tenancy in common (TIC), an arrangement that allows each buyer to own a share of the building. Last fall, the new owners invoked the Ellis Act, a state law that allows landlords to evict their tenants if they want to withdraw the property from the rental market. “The Ellis Act is such a disgusting thing,” said Bernard Dethiers, a building tenant of more than 30 years who described Cunningham and her son as family. “It’s just immoral to do the Ellis Act. I mean, it’s perfectly legal. But it’s immoral.” Two of the new owners previously rented a unit in the building before buying into the TIC, according to Cunningham, which she said makes the ordeal even more uncomfortable. “It’s neighbors evicting neighbors,” Cunningham said. Dethiers – originally from France – said he also received an offer from the ownership group to buy into the TIC, but refused. “What was going to happen to my neighbors?” he said. “I just couldn’t do anything that would hurt them or be involved in any kind of eviction.” Under the terms of the Ellis Act, the tenants are supposed to move out by November. But they decided to fight the eviction, seeking help from the Tenderloin Housing Clinic, a nonprofit that offers legal aid to low-income San Francisco residents. Steve Collier, the organization’s managing attorney, said he believes the Ellis Act shouldn’t be used as an eviction tool for brand-new owners. “We find that the Ellis Act primarily is used by people who just bought a building,” Collier said. “It’s simply used as a vehicle to displace rent-controlled tenants.” If forced to leave, Collier said his clients would be hard-pressed to find a home in the city that they can afford. One of his clients currently pays about $600 a month, he said, and nobody in the building pays more than $1,300. While the Ellis Act requires landlords to offer relocation payments to their displaced tenants – which vary in amount depending on the circumstances of each renter – Collier said they’re not enough for many rent-controlled tenants to afford market-rate housing. According to Zumper, the median rental price for a one-bedroom apartment now hovers north of $4,000. “I think this would be absolutely the end of the North Beach life for sure, and perhaps even San Francisco,” Cunningham said. Chui said she’s hoping to find housing assistance from the city, but Collier said that’s in short supply and even harder to find for multigenerational households like hers. “I am very flustered,” she said. “I don’t know what to do.” In a statement shared with NBC Bay Area through their attorney, the owners of the building described themselves as “long term North Beach renters” who are legally pursuing home ownership “in a city with an evergreen housing shortage.” “[The owners] are not developers speculating on the A-I bubble,” they said in the statement. “They are families looking for a way to raise their young children in the city they love.” “The city provides housing opportunities for tenants who are displaced in this way, and the owners hope that the tenants avail themselves of these opportunities,” they added. Both sides now find themselves fighting over the eviction in court. The building’s owners filed a lawsuit against their tenants in April – before the tenants were required to move out – seeking to resolve several disputes over the eviction and limit some of the potential legal defenses the tenants might later raise in court. This week, the tenants filed a cross-complaint against the building’s owners, accusing them of housing discrimination and other civil violations. According to the cross-complaint, “only the caucasian tenants in the property” were given offers to buy into the ownership group. “We believe that kind of discrimination, either in effect or on purpose, is illegal,” Collier said. “None of the Asian families were offered to buy into their unit. Meagan Cunningham and her family, who are also of mixed heritage, were not offered, even though they expressed an interest.” NBC Bay Area requested comment from the owners on the allegations in the cross-complaint, but it was not addressed in their statement. For Dethiers, the fight represents something beyond his own fate. “We do it for us,” Dethiers said. “We do it also for other tenants all over the city who are under rent control.”
headlines.source: Christine Ni, Michael Bott, Raginee Sudhir Chaurey, Audrey Asistio and Robbie Beasom

headlines.title: Wastewater data shows COVID-19 surge in several Bay Area communities
headlines.description: Wastewater data shows COVID-19 rates are on a “summer surge” in several Bay Area communities. The increase is showing up in wastewater from Marin County to the South Bay, giving health officials a sense of both where and how much COVID-19 is circulating in the community. While doctors say there are still reasons to be cautious, they’re also seeing signs this “summer surge” could look very different from those of the past. “It’s several fold higher than it was about a month ago and test positivity is increasing,” UCSF Professor of Medicine and Infectious Disease Specialist Peter Chin-Hong said. Palo Alto, Sunnyvale, San Jose and Marin are among the areas seeing high or rising levels of the virus; San Francisco is seeing its highest wastewater levels since last September, but hospitalizations for the virus remain very low. “It gives us a good sense for how much COVID-19 is being transmitted in the community. So, over the last few months, we’ve seen a sustained increase in COVID-19 levels, suggesting we are about to see a summer wave of COVID transmission,” Krishna Surasi, assistant public health officer and communicable disease controller for the Santa Clara County Public Health Department said. “We’ve been seeing a decline in hospitalizations over time and that’s because many people are seeing waves and waves of COVID-19 so their immune system is experienced,” Chin-Hong said. Now, with a growing number of schools back in session, doctors are watching to see whether more close contact drives transmission even higher. “With heat waves and extreme weather a lot of people gather indoors now for air conditioning, etc, and that brings a lot of noses and mouths together, so infection can spread that way,” Chin-Hong said. There’s also a new variant in the mix. It’s called the Cicada variant, and Dr. Chin-Hong says it’s showing more mutations than previous variants — another factor health departments are watching as COVID-19 continues to evolve. For now, health officials say the basics still matter, especially as students return to classrooms. “Washing your hands frequently, practicing good hygiene, and if you need to cough or sneeze do that into your elbow so you are not spreading it around the room, stay up to date on COVID-19 vaccines,” Surasi said. Experts say the next few weeks will be key in determining whether this is simply another summer wave or the beginning of a larger surge. A new COVID-19 vaccine is expected this fall. The CDC recommends an updated COVID-19 vaccine each year, with the timing based on the individual’s age and risk, but Chin-Hong says older adults and people at high risk for severe illness who are concerned about the current rise can talk with their doctor about getting a booster sooner.

headlines.title: Parents, neighbors frustrated by traffic outside San Jose elementary school
headlines.description: Parents and neighbors near a San Jose elementary school say the first days back to school have brought a traffic nightmare following the merger of two campuses. Lowell Elementary School merged with Washington Elementary School this year, and parents say pickups and drop-offs at Washington have not gone smoothly. Neighbors describe the area outside the school before and after classes as congested, with some drivers blocking driveways and double parking. “A lot of parents, we tell them, ‘Please don’t block my driveway.’ And they get mad and they get angry and they yell at us,” said Linda Cortez, who lives across the street from the school. “It’s awful. It’s terrible.” Cortez said the congestion can make it difficult for other vehicles, including fire trucks and school buses, to get through. Because of school closures, San Jose Unified transferred Lowell Elementary students to Washington Elementary, increasing the number of students at the campus and the amount of traffic around the school. The Villamor family transferred from Lowell and is among the families now looking for parking each day. “Most of the time. All of the time. There is no space for you to park anywhere,” parent Maria Elena Villamor said when asked whether she has to double park. “You have to wait for people to pass, to find space.” Villamor said she has seen police issuing tickets this week. She said she understands neighbors’ frustrations but needs to park and walk her son to school to make sure he gets inside safely. San Jose Unified said it provides daily buses to pick up and drop off students from Lowell, but very few families are choosing that option and are instead driving to the new school. In a statement to NBC Bay Area, San Jose Unified School District said: “As we begin a new school year at Washington Elementary, we are excited for the increased opportunities that a larger student body offers to our students, staff, and families. At the same time, we recognize that, with Washington Elementary’s enrollment returning closer to where it was ten years ago, the traffic patterns in the surrounding neighborhood are affected. We take the concerns of our families and neighbors seriously, and we are committed to ensuring that arrival and dismissal are safe and efficient for everyone. “We proactively worked with the City of San José over the summer to establish a new loading zone to improve traffic flow. We also began collaboration with Councilmember Tordillos office on exploring opportunities for additional pedestrian safety improvements, including enhanced crosswalk measures around the campus. We want to thank Councilmember Tordillos and his office for their partnership and responsiveness. “We have already seen meaningful improvement in traffic flow during drop-off and pick-up this week. The feedback we are receiving from families has been positive, and neighbors have also thanked school staff for reinforcing traffic expectations and helping keep vehicles moving. We are grateful to the San José Police Department for its partnership and presence in the area, including enforcement of traffic laws around the school. “We are collaborating with the City of San José to conduct joint-observations at pick-up and drop-off during the first few weeks of school to identify additional opportunities for improvement. We will continue to monitor traffic conditions, listen to feedback from our families and neighbors, and make adjustments where needed as our school community settles into the new school year.” Neighbors say they just want their streets back.

headlines.title: Multiple families displaced after residential fire in Suisun City
headlines.description: A fire that burned through homes in Suisun City on Thursday displaced several families with children, according to Mayor Alma Hernandez. Suisun City Fire Department crews arrived early Thursday morning at the 600 block of School Street on the west side of the city, where multiple structures were burning, according to a statement from the department. Roughly 10 individuals, including toddlers, were displaced in the blaze, said Hernandez, who was at the scene for several hours after the fire started. There were no injuries, she said. Hernandez noted that wind was a factor in the quick spread of the fire, which she estimated burned through “four or five residences.” “Suisun City is known for its ‘west wind’ — that’s what Suisun means,” said Hernandez in a phone call, referring to the local indigenous Patwin origins of the city’s name. The American Red Cross, which provides housing assistance, food, and financial relief for victims of fires, arrived at the scene around 2 a.m., and is currently helping to place those affected into temporary housing and hotels, according to Hernandez. Some of the displaced individuals have opted to stay with family nearby until a long-term option becomes available. Local crews were assisted by fire departments from Fairfield, Benicia, Travis Air Force Base and Vallejo. Suisun City Fire Department remained on the scene through Thursday afternoon assessing damage and carrying out an investigation into what caused the blaze.

headlines.title: California prisons fail to stop guards from sexually abusing women, Justice Department finds
headlines.description: California ‘s prison system has systematically failed to protect incarcerated women from sexual abuse and harassment by guards, the U.S. Department of Justice said Thursday. The federal investigation also found that California’s corrections department failed to provide victims with a way to report sexual abuse and harassment without retaliation. On top of that, staff who were tasked with investigating the misconduct were often themselves accused of sexual abuse or harassment. The investigation, which began during the Biden administration, focused on two state prisons: the Central California Women’s Facility in Chowchilla and the California Institution for Women in Chino. It uncovered numerous instances where guards regularly sexually abused incarcerated women. In at least one instance, a guard was convicted of rampant abuse over roughly a decade and sentenced to 224 years in prison. State says it’s making improvements. Advocates say it’s not enough. The California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation said in a statement that it “enforces a zero-tolerance policy as mandated by the federal Prison Rape Elimination Act,” a federal law passed in 2003 designed to prevent sexual assaults in prisons. The state agency also said that audits conducted by independent entities trained by the DOJ found the two prisons were in compliance with federal standards as recently as 2024 and 2025. “CDCR is fully committed to supporting victims of sexual assault and ensuring safe avenues exist for both incarcerated persons and staff to confidentially report misconduct,” spokesperson Will Matthews wrote in an email. Over the course of the DOJ investigation, the prison agency independently investigated and prosecuted both staff and incarcerated people who violated federal rape prevention laws, he added. Emily Wonder, who works for Sister Warriors, which advocates for incarcerated women and transgender people, said state audits evaluate prison conditions based on a very “low bar” that allows abuse and neglect to slip through the cracks. “It’s not a very strong protection mechanism in general,” Wonder said. Sister Warriors, other groups and lawmakers are pushing for additional legislation to bolster protections for women, increase opportunities for reporting misconduct and improve transparency. Federal authorities echoed that assessment on Thursday, saying that there weren’t sufficient mechanisms for victims to come forward. Women don’t have resources to report assaults, Justice Department says Women were told to report misconduct on an online system that wasn’t confidential and that accused officers had access to, according to Harmeet K. Dhillon, assistant attorney general for the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. Dhillon said that women are “fully aware of this gap in confidentiality, and this serves as a deterrent from women reporting this misconduct.” She named at least one sergeant whose job was to investigate misconduct who was himself sentenced to 15 years in prison after pleading guilty to receiving child sexual abuse images at work. “The upshot of our investigation is that California’s prison system, when it comes to women, has inadequate systems in place to deter, detect, and hold accountable rampant sexual misconduct and assault on female prisoners,” Dhillon said at a news conference in Los Angeles on Thursday. The Associated Press has previously exposed similar patterns of rampant abuse by federal prison staff against women held in a Dublin, California, facility that at the time was nicknamed the “rape club.” The prison was closed following the AP investigation. Justice Department sets a deadline to address problems The federal government on Thursday gave California’s prison system 49 days to remediate the conditions that enabled the rampant abuse, warning that a failure to do so could result in civil litigation. The measures include expanded camera coverage, enhanced confidential reporting channels and strengthened investigative protocols. The corrections department was implementing many of those changes before the federal investigation, Matthews said. But Wonder, whose organization has participated in a state-funded working group with the corrections department since 2023, said that advocates “haven’t seen any meaningful changes” despite regular meetings and pressure from the public. “We’ve been really frustrated, feeling like we’re spinning our wheels,” Wonder said. U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli, appointed by President Donald Trump as the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, said California has to take action. “The State must confront the persistent failure of its own employees to prevent and address sexual abuse at these facilities,” Essayli said in a statement, “and the systemic breakdowns that have permitted these conditions to persist.”

headlines.title: San Jose State students get unlimited Bay Area transit with Clipper BayPass
headlines.description: Getting to campus, internships and jobs is about to become more affordable for San Jose State University students, with unlimited transit rides across the Bay Area beginning Saturday. Students began signing up Thursday for the Clipper BayPass, which gives them access to VTA, BART, AC Transit and Caltrain, as well as participating rail and ferry services. University and transit leaders said the program is aimed at increasing transportation equity for San Jose State’s 32,000 students while opening up more internship and employment opportunities and giving students a chance to explore all nine Bay Area counties. “Internships these days are income, and that income is experience,” Associated Students President Ma’Kayla Akin said, adding that the program could help students gain experience before entering the workforce. The Clipper BayPass is available to full- and part-time students and is valid throughout the nine-county Bay Area. While students will not pay for individual rides through the program, they agreed to contribute about $49 per year in student fees toward it. University leaders said they will work to build support and increase enrollment and usage as they consider the program’s future and the possibility of expanding it.

headlines.title: Oakland's Home of Chicken and Waffles to close after more than 20 years
headlines.description: A beloved Oakland institution is closing its doors after more than two decades. Home of Chicken and Waffles near Jack London Square will serve its final meals later this month. The restaurant opened in 2004 and is known for its fried chicken, golden waffles and Southern comfort food. Owner Derreck Johnson said the restaurant was never just about the food, but also about bringing people together and giving back to the community. A reason for the closure was not given. Johnson said he is looking ahead to his next chapter and plans to announce more details in the coming months.

headlines.title: BART says cracks on new fleet gearboxes ‘not a safety concern'
headlines.description: Cracks have been found on the gearboxes of dozens of BART’s Fleet of the Future train cars – sometimes after only one year in service – according to a new analysis ordered by state regulators and obtained by NBC Bay Area’s Investigative Unit under the state’s Public Records Act. Both BART and the train maker, Alstom, stress that while cracks have been found on the top covers of the new fleet gearboxes, they are not a safety concern. They say a redesigned, crack-resistant gearbox top cover is now undergoing testing. But one expert says any cracks must be considered a red flag, given the vital function of the gearbox. “The gearbox is a high-performance system,” said Don Mullen, a former BART engineer who worked on its legacy fleet. Mullen says that the gearbox functions the same as a transmission in a car, serving to automatically control the spinning of train axles and wheels. He said the old fleet shared the same gearbox design, but its gearbox was rarely a problem. Maintenance logs reviewed by NBC Bay Area’s Investigative Unit indicate leaks of gearbox lubricant have been found along with cracking. Any unchecked leak could potentially compromise the gearbox’s critical speed-control function, Mullen says, and should be considered a major concern. “Leaking oil out of a gear case, analogous to a transmission in your car, is not a good thing,” Mullen said, calling on more tests to assure that the gearbox integrity is not being compromised in the new fleet. “It can’t be ignored,” Mullen stressed. The study that identified the cracking issue was performed by a third-party consultant. Records obtained by NBC Bay Area show it was launched at the order of the state’s Public Utilities Commission back in 2022. Regulators intervened after an anonymous insider pointed to concerns raised by BART’s own engineers about safety impacts to the gearbox of a glitch that has long plagued the new fleet — sudden braking during wet weather. In slippery conditions, BART says, new fleet car sensors kick on, activating emergency brakes on all cars at once. The sudden braking grinds flat spots that force entire trains in to have wheels resurfaced. At a cost of $8,000 per car, according to BART documents. BART engineers complained to the trainmaker about the flat problem, documents show. They also indicate engineers warned about the potential damage to the gearbox over time due to all the sudden braking. BART cited the sudden wet-weather braking issue as one of the reasons it stopped accepting new train cars from Alstom back in 2021. But a year later, BART resumed shipments, telling regulators that slowing speeds in wet weather should resolve the issue. But in 2022, the insider contacted rail regulators with the CPUC, pointing them to the concerns previously raised by BART’s own engineers over the potential risk to the gearbox from repeated sudden braking, according to CPUC documents. BART documents show its engineers told Alstom at the time that the risk to the gearbox from stresses from sudden braking over the long term must be considered a potential Level One concern, until proven otherwise. A Level One concern is defined as one that poses “an immediate safety or reliability risk.” To address delays associated with the braking, BART spent $4 million last year to reprogram trains to slow down automatically in braking-related trouble spots. However, BART maintenance records reviewed by NBC Bay Area show dozens of cars still needed to have their wheels resurfaced last winter because of sudden braking. The cost is currently being borne under the warranty. The gearbox risk study, which relies on computer analysis, noted that cracks have formed on a “large number” of gearbox covers due to “high stress and insufficient fatigue safety factors.” The housing of the gearbox met safety margins, the report found, but the cover material did not meet minimum fatigue safety standards. The cracking failures began showing up, the study found, after trains were in service for a year. The report concluded the “likely cause of the cover crack failures” was stress, both from braking in service and the stress inflected by tightening down the covers during installation. In a statement, BART confirmed that so far, more than 200 covers have been replaced on the new fleet. But didn’t specify whether all of them were cracked. It did acknowledge gearbox cracks can cause “minor oil weeping” that’s addressed in service. BART did not address the findings of the gearbox analysis in detail, however, saying only: “BART does not consider this a safety issue.” Alstom said in a statement that it conducted “a comprehensive analysis” and determined the gearbox cover issue “has no impact on safety or performance of the trains,” and added it has enhanced the cover design “to address the cracking.” But Mullen says the only way to know whether the new fleet’s gearboxes are, in fact, safe is to do field tests under the extreme forces of sudden braking, rather than rely solely on computer modeling to rule out the risk of a catastrophic failure, like a derailment. “You need to be conservative,’’ Mullen said. “The public’s trusting you. They bought the system. They paid for it with their tax money. They use it and assume it always works.” State regulators say BART has told them it expects field testing to be done next year.
headlines.source: Jaxon Van Derbeken and Jeremy Carroll

headlines.title: Allowing cars back on SF's Great Highway could cost more than $10M, controller says
headlines.description: The San Francisco Office of the Controller wrote in an analysis this week that Proposition G, a ballot measure to let cars back on the Great Highway, would cost the city millions of dollars if it passes in November. Making the road suitable for cars would “significantly increase the cost of government by approximately $9.8 million in one-time capital costs and by approximately $500,000 to $1.9 million annually,” wrote Deputy Controller ChiaYu Ma in a letter to the city’s Department of Elections on Tuesday. Prop G will ask all San Francisco voters if they want to allow cars back on the coastal road during weekdays and keep it as a park on the weekends — which supporters of the measure call the “compromise.” The compromise went into effect during the COVID-19 pandemic when fewer cars were on the roads and the city wanted to have more open space for the public when social distancing was needed. Voters then decided to turn the 2-mile stretch of the Great Highway into a permanent park during the November 2024 election, officially closing it to cars. Streetlights at intersections were removed, and park structures and amenities began popping up. However, a group of voters and residents on San Francisco’s west side, where a majority voted against the closure, started a movement to reopen the Great Highway back to cars and return to the “compromise.” The group’s measure received enough signatures to qualify for the upcoming November election. But the Controller’s Office estimates that adding in new traffic signals, restriping the road, erecting signage, and removing park amenities could cost the city about $10 million. Additional annual costs for sand removal could cost up to about $2 million annually. Friends of Sunset Dunes, the group fighting to keep the road as a permanent park, launched a campaign in response called “No on G: Save Sunset Dunes Park.” “Proposition G will charge San Franciscans millions of dollars to close a beloved park,” said the campaign’s manager Lucas Lux in a statement. “This expensive ballot measure would waste taxpayer money to replace a thriving park with a failed road, a section of which has closed anyway due to coastal erosion.” But Albert Chow, a west side resident and firm supporter of restoring the compromise, thinks that potential safety risks of not allowing cars back on the roadway could outweigh the financial cost. In an interview, Chow mentioned concerns over road and traffic safety and congestion that could increase on other roads in the Sunset District if more people move into the area under the Family Zoning Plan, which rezoned parts of the area to allow for the construction of denser housing. The Sunset District is bordered by the Great Highway to the west, and much of the roads within the district are referred to as the “avenues.” “I think that at some point, somebody’s going to get hurt because they’re driving through the avenues as a direct result of the road being closed and forcing faster cars to go through the avenues, which were never meant to take that kind of traffic,” Chow said. “Is $9.8 million better to abate that? Yeah, I think so.” The Controller’s Office also added in its letter that additional costs are possible since a new plaza is being planned at the intersection of Sloat Boulevard and the Great Highway as part of the Ocean Beach Climate Change Adaptation Project. The project involves structural improvements and recreational elements in the area to help address shoreline erosion and sea level rise. Erecting new traffic signals at the intersection could result in added costs from having redesign elements of the plaza. The office also wrote that it estimates additional costs at an “undetermined” amount involved in applying for a coastal development permit, a process that includes possible studies and other requirements in order to allow cars back on the road. A full financial analysis of the measure with possible revisions will be provided in the city’s voter pamphlet for the November election.
